question: In standard Java source files, what constraint governs the relationship between the file name and the classes defined within it?

options.text: Every class declared inside a file must possess its own distinct public static void main method.
A top-level public class must be declared in a source file whose base name matches the class name exactly.
Source filenames are completely independent of class names because the compiler derives naming from package headers.
A single .java compilation unit may contain multiple top-level public classes if their names share a common prefix.

explanation: Java requires that any top-level public class reside in a .java file with the identical base name. The belief that filenames are independent of class names overlooks the compiler's strict translation unit lookup rules, and multiple public top-level classes in a single file are rejected at compile time.

question: Which statement accurately describes how non-static instance fields are maintained in Java?

options.text: Top-level classes can define instance variables only when declared with default package-private visibility.
Non-static instance fields can only be declared inside classes that define a public static void main method.
Each instantiated object allocates and maintains its own separate copy of all non-static instance variables.
The class declaration itself directly stores and accumulates instance field values as a global table.

explanation: A class serves as a blueprint; each concrete instance created from that class gets its own separate memory allocation for instance variables. The belief that the class itself stores instance values confuses class definitions with instantiated objects.

question: What determines whether a compiled Java class can be launched directly as the entry point of a program?

options.text: The class must contain a valid public static void main(String[] args) method declaration.
The class must directly store instance field values without requiring object instantiation.
Any class with at least one public instance method can be executed directly by the java runtime.
The class must be declared in a file that contains at least two distinct public class declarations.

explanation: The Java Virtual Machine specifies that execution entry begins at a public static void main(String[] args) method. The assumption that any class can execute directly without a main method violates the entry point specification.

question: What happens if a developer attempts to declare two top-level public classes within a single file named Alpha.java?

options.text: The code compiles cleanly but requires a main method inside both declarations to execute.
The compiler compiles both classes provided that Alpha is written as the primary class.
The compiler issues a compile-time error stating that the second class must be declared in its own file.
The compiler creates a single merged class combining both bodies under the Alpha name.

explanation: A compilation unit can contain at most one top-level public class. Having two top-level public classes in the same source file causes javac to report a compile-time error. Java does not allow multiple public top-level classes per file.

options.text: A compile-time error occurs because class First is public and should be declared in First.java.
A runtime error occurs because First does not contain a main method.
It compiles cleanly and prints Running when executed.
It compiles only if First is modified to be an abstract class.

explanation: Because First is a top-level public class inside Test.java, javac rejects the file with an error stating class First is public and should be declared in a file named First.java. A file can contain only one top-level public class.

options.text: Compilation error because Counter is declared in the same file as public class Main.
0 0 because instance fields cannot be reassigned outside the class declaration.
5 5 because instance fields are stored centrally in the Counter class definition.
5 0 because each instance of Counter possesses its own independent count variable.

explanation: Non-static fields belong to object instances, not the class definition. Modifying c1.count to 5 affects only c1, leaving c2.count at its default value 0. The belief that c2 reflects c1's value mistakenly assumes the class itself stores instance state.

options.text: 5 2 because method grow modifies instance state only on the calling object b1.
2 2 because instance methods cannot mutate fields declared within class bodies.
Compilation error because Box lacks a public static void main method.
5 5 because invoking grow modifies the shared class template definition.

explanation: Invoking grow() on b1 mutates b1.length to 5, while b2 remains an independent instance with length 2. Thinking that b2.length also changes confuses instance state with shared class variables.

options.text: Compilation error because Worker does not define its own main entry method.
Compilation error because the file name App.java does not match public class Runner.
It compiles and prints Work because the file name is automatically reassigned to Runner.
It compiles cleanly because top-level class names are independent of file names.

explanation: If a compilation unit contains a public class (Runner), the file name must match that class name (Runner.java). Naming the file App.java causes javac to reject the file. Top-level public class names must strictly match their file names.

options.text: Compilation error because Account is not declared as a public class.
100 150 because a1 and a2 represent distinct instances stored in the Account class.
100 100 because deposit is an instance method unable to alter reference state.
150 150 because both variables reference the identical object in heap memory.

explanation: The assignment Account a2 = a1 copies the reference, so both a1 and a2 point to the same Account object. Mutating balance through a2.deposit(50) reflects across both reference variables, printing '150 150'. Thinking they hold separate balances fails to grasp reference assignment versus object instantiation.

options.text: It compiles successfully, but java Solution fails at runtime with Could not find or load main class Solution.
It compiles and prints Helper because the runtime defaults execution to Core.
It fails to compile because Helper cannot be invoked without its own main method.
Compilation error because neither class inside Solution.java is declared public.

explanation: A source file can omit public classes and name itself Solution.java without compile error. However, javac produces Helper.class and Core.class (no Solution.class). Running java Solution fails at runtime because no Solution class exists. Running java Core would succeed.

options.text: Compilation error because a class definition cannot declare a field of its own class type.
Compilation error because Node must be declared public in its own file Node.java.
1 1 because nested instance allocations share the top-level class definition's field storage.
1 2 because each new Node allocates an independent instance with distinct val storage.

explanation: A class definition can contain self-referential fields. Each evaluation of new Node() allocates a fresh object with its own instance variable val. Thus n1.val is 1 and n1.next.val is 2, printing '1 2'. The belief that recursive structures share field storage in the class definition confuses class metadata with instance allocation.

question: Which statement correctly differentiates package-private classes from public classes defined in the same translation unit?

options.text: A source file can contain multiple public classes as long as package-private classes are placed after them.
Package-private classes can be executed directly from the terminal without declaring a main method.
A source file may define multiple package-private classes alongside at most one public class.
Package-private classes automatically store all field state directly inside the class definition table.

explanation: In Java, a single source file may declare at most one public top-level class, but it can declare any number of non-public (package-private) top-level classes. The claim that multiple public classes can coexist in one file violates translation unit rules.
